mode: cover states as free toggles, not a guided ladder
description: The support-removal system has a small finite set of meaningful states (issue #1's ladder: audio-only → EN visible → both → FR-only → …), but the UI exposes them as independent cover-EN/cover-FR toggles the learner must puzzle out — easy to derail into 'what state am I in?'. Present the finite states as one legible guided progression (a stepper the method advances) instead of free toggles.
example_quotes: could easily confuse the user given the finite states — and not derailing while trying to figure this out

description: Unusual method moves (shadowing, the recall wave, the cover ladder, transfer) drop the learner straight into the exercise with no first-encounter introduction — no 'here's what this is, why it works, what to do' to earn buy-in before asking for effort. First-run concept intros (once, dismissible, progressive-disclosure style) prevent the confusion the owner is nervous about; pairs with the jargon findings (the terms would land after the concept is introduced).
example_quotes: maybe introduce this concept to get buy-in from the learner first because I'm nervous they will get confused
transfer step: 'help them recall prior knowledge, and understand what the schema of construction means' — activate the owned construction before demanding production

mode: exercises show the whole set instead of chunking
description: Exercise steps (recall especially) present all items at once with one detached input at the bottom, instead of chunking: one phrase at a time, the input adjacent to where the learner is looking, complete all N, then advance. Progressive disclosure applied to exercise structure — reduces visual search, keeps attempt and stimulus together, and unifies with the mobile swipe-sequential architecture (same principle, all viewports).
example_quotes: making this closer to where the user sees this visually… only do 1 phrase at a time and have them do all 11 and then hit next ('progressive disclosure' or potential chunking of exercises)

description: Onboarding/intake steps don't actively carry the learner through their cognitive load: no short feedback loops that pay back each action, and no motivational framing strong enough to supersede the effort of completing intake. Progressive disclosure + instant per-action response + why-this-is-worth-it framing, applied per section.
example_quotes: progressive disclosure and short feedback loops that engage the user's brain… overcome the cognitive load of doing this intake process
help the user overcome motivation that will supersede the cognitive load required to complete onboarding

description: The in-lesson header/chrome ('AU CAFÉ · STEP 1 · LISTEN') reads as generic app chrome rather than signaling you've entered a distinct session mode. Either keep it strictly consistent with the app shell or commit the other way: style the whole lesson shell as a 'game mode' the learner visibly enters and exits — which pairs with the preview's dark stage and the character-world direction.
example_quotes: keep this consistent or update the style of how this is rendered to make this seem like its a 'game mode'

mode: mobile needs its own interaction architecture
description: Mobile is currently a compressed port of desktop. Two rules emerged: (1) lesson steps are no-scroll, swipe-sequential full-viewport cards; scroll is reserved for rare, deliberate deep-dives. (2) OPEN QUESTION, the hard one: the finger-parallel-reading technique itself — pointing at both languages at once — may not be tenable on a narrow viewport at all; mobile may need a re-derivation of the parallel-reading method (e.g., thumb-anchored pair stepping, alternating reveal) rather than a shrunken spread. Decide the mobile-native form of the method before styling anything.
example_quotes: the user wants no scrolling when in this part — we should focus on sequentially moving via swiping and then occasionally and sparingly… a deeper dive via scrolling… only when it's important to leave a lasting impression
what mobile application development would do to handle porting our instructional design theory about parallel reading… by pointing your finger to read. but is that really tenable for mobile.

description: Informational, no-action text (interaction hints like 'Track both lines together. Tap a line to replay it.') renders as plain body copy indistinguishable from content. Hints need a distinct callout treatment — a visual grammar that says 'this is guidance for working the learning UX', separate from both content and controls.
example_quotes: signal information text with no action using a callout if I need a hint to work with the learning UX
